result.summary: Pausanias describes sites near Corinth, including the temple of Aphrodite, the fountain given by Asopus to Sisyphus, and the river Asopus with its traditions. He then turns to Tenea and a burnt temple on the road to Sicyon, and gives the Sicyonian line of early kings.

scenes.title: Aphrodite's temple and Sisyphus's fountain
scenes.summary: On Acro-Corinthus stands a temple of Aphrodite with statues. A fountain behind it was said to be Asopus's payment to Sisyphus for telling where Ægina went.
scenes.stakes: Sisyphus suffers punishment in Hades for betraying Zeus's secret.

scenes.title: The river Asopus and its daughters
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the course of the Asopus, its daughters' names, and claims that it and other rivers came from distant rivers.

scenes.title: Tenea and the burnt temple
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Tenea, whose people claim Trojan descent, and a burnt temple on the Sicyon road.

scenes.title: Early kings of Sicyon
scenes.summary: The Sicyonians list their early kings from Ægialeus down to Coronus and his sons.

analysis.text: Pausanias blends local legends, rival claims and his own scepticism, as when he doubts Sisyphus's punishment is credible.
Cities such as Tenea and Sicyon asserted prestige through legendary founders and royal genealogies reaching back to heroic times.

fun_facts.text: Acrocorinth still has a spring, often identified with Upper Pirene, mentioned in the discussion of the fountain.

language_notes.text: Zeus carried off Ægina, Asopus's daughter; Sisyphus, the legendary king of Corinth, informed on him, which is why he was punished in Hades.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted; here Sisyphus condescended to give the information.
Pirene was Corinth's famous spring, said in myth to have been a woman who wept herself into a fountain.
"Indigenous" means native to the place; the claim is that the river came from abroad.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet (about 185 metres).
"Autochthon" means born from the land itself, a native who did not migrate in.
Pelops gave his name to the Peloponnese and was linked with the founding of the Olympic games, so this dates Apis's greatness to early times.

context_notes.text: Acro-Corinthus was the steep citadel hill above Corinth, long associated with the worship of Aphrodite.
Ilithyia was the goddess who presided over childbirth.
Pyrrhus (Neoptolemus), son of Achilles, was a Trojan War hero said to have wandered widely after the war.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias's sceptical aside "if indeed this is credible" shows him distancing himself from the myth he reports.
Pausanias reports traditions with phrases like "there is a tradition," acting as a careful collector who does not vouch for them.
The narrator's personal verdict of "most marvellous" shows his taste for wonders and builds anticipation for the story.
